name: Consistency
summary: Readers see coherent, correct data under a well-defined consistency model — from strong ACID guarantees to intentionally eventual views.
description: Consistency is whether readers observe data that agrees with itself and with the writes that produced it, under a stated model. Strongly consistent designs use ACID transactions, single sources of truth, and isolation so every reader sees a coherent snapshot. Eventually consistent designs trade immediate agreement for speed and availability, accepting that different readers may briefly disagree. The right level is a deliberate choice, not an accident.

mechanisms.name: ACID table transactions
mechanisms.note: Open table formats commit atomic snapshots with isolation, so readers never see partial writes and concurrent writers do not corrupt state.

mechanisms.name: Single source of truth
mechanisms.note: Routing all writes through one authoritative store or golden record removes conflicting copies that would otherwise drift apart.

mechanisms.name: Exactly-once processing
mechanisms.note: Transactional stream processing with checkpointing ensures each event affects results once, preventing duplicate-driven inconsistency.

mechanisms.name: Referential integrity and constraints
mechanisms.note: Enforcing keys, uniqueness, and relationships at load time keeps dimensions and facts coherent so joins never dangle.

mechanisms.name: Snapshot isolation for readers
mechanisms.note: Serving queries from committed snapshots means long-running reads see a stable, self-consistent view even as writers append.

manifestations.statement: Transactional loads into conformed dimensions and facts give every reporting query a single, referentially coherent view of the business.
A normalized 3NF core enforced with keys and constraints is the single source of truth, so dependent marts stay mutually consistent by construction.
Atomic Iceberg snapshot commits with snapshot isolation mean many engines all read one coherent, self-consistent copy of the data.
ACID commits on the table format let silver and gold present consistent snapshots even while bronze is continuously appended.
Golden-record resolution collapses conflicting source copies into one authoritative version, which is the entire point of the hub.
Deterministic SQL transforms with tested keys and one warehouse of record keep staging and marts internally coherent.
Hash-keyed hubs and links plus load-once satellites preserve a consistent, fully auditable integrated view across many sources.
Warehouse transactions keep transformed models coherent, but freshness lag between load and transform means readers can briefly see stale-but-consistent data.
Single-node in-process execution gives simple transactional coherence, though it is one process, not a concurrency-hardened multi-writer store.
Frequent atomic commits keep each table snapshot consistent, but readers between commits see minutes-fresh views rather than the very latest events.
OLAP serving stays internally consistent per query, but replication lag and async ingestion mean fresh rows may arrive out of order across replicas.
The mirror is eventually consistent by design: warehouse rows converge on source state only after change events are merged, so brief divergence is expected.
Everything-is-a-stream favors low latency over immediate agreement, so downstream views are eventually consistent as events flow and reprocess.
Independent consumers apply events on their own timelines, so cross-service state is eventually consistent — a deliberate exchange for decoupling and speed.
The speed layer serves approximate fresh results while the batch layer corrects them, so readers accept temporary inconsistency until reconciliation.
Unified profiles are coherent once resolved, but identity stitching across async sources means a profile can lag or briefly reflect conflicting inputs.
A federated query stitches independent sources with no shared transaction, so legs read at different moments and results can be internally inconsistent.
Loose files with no atomic commits or constraints let partial writes and duplicate landings coexist, so coherence is not guaranteed to readers.
Pushed records converge on downstream SaaS state only after each sync, and per-tool APIs apply updates independently, so activation is eventually consistent at best.
Because partners read one shared copy rather than exchanging extracts, everyone sees the same source of truth, though governed join outputs are point-in-time rather than transactionally live.
The underlying data stays coherent, but masking, tokenization, and row-level policies mean different roles see deliberately different — yet internally consistent — projections of the same records.
A single governed definition per metric is compiled into every query, so revenue or churn resolves to the same number in every dashboard, notebook, and API by construction.
Per-tenant isolation keeps each customer's view coherent within its boundary, though shared pipelines and async ingestion mean freshness can lag across tenants.
Data contracts keep each domain's published product internally coherent, but there is no global transaction across products, so cross-domain joins are only eventually aligned.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Coordination protocols, locking, and quorum acknowledgements add round-trips and waiting before a write is confirmed, directly increasing response latency.

tradeoffs.title: Availability
tradeoffs.note: Under the CAP theorem, choosing strong consistency means the system must reject or block operations during network partitions rather than serve possibly-stale data.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Serializable isolation and global ordering serialize conflicting operations, limiting the parallelism a system can exploit and capping sustainable throughput.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Transactional ACID guarantees require extra bookkeeping, replication acknowledgements, and often over-provisioned coordinators, raising the compute cost per operation.
